paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Collins took place in Wichita, Kansas, on the night of May 26, 1888, when a report spread that a mob would storm the county jail and hang Collins, a Black man accused of raping a widow. Sheriff Hays armed guards, a militia company stood ready and a party of Black men gathered to protect the prisoner, and no mob appeared. Collins was later tried twice, convicted and sentenced to nine years in the penitentiary.

According to a wire report dated May 22, a Black man entered a widow's house in the north part of Wichita at about two o'clock that morning, choked her unconscious and assaulted her. The woman, named in the Wichita papers as Mrs. Standley and in the wire as Sophia Stanley, lived on North Mosley with a five-year-old child. Three Black men brought before her that day were not identified, and the dispatch said the excitement was accompanied by "the usual talk of lynching."

An old man of seventy was arrested and then discharged before Officer Webking arrested Collins, whom Mrs. Standley said she recognized as her assailant. She swore out a warrant against him at Justice Hammond's court the day after his arrest.

At about ten o'clock on the night of May 26, a report spread on the street that a mob was about to take Collins from the jail and hang him. Sheriff Hays asked for help and armed as many men as he thought necessary, announcing that a mob "might expect a very warm reception." Crowds gathered around the jail to watch, the militia company Co. A, K.N.G., was on the ground, and a party of Black men announced that they had come to prevent any harm to the prisoner.

Scouts sent through the town learned nothing of the would-be lynchers' numbers or whereabouts. The Eagle credited the general preparation with discouraging any movement, and the night passed without the mob appearing.

Justice Hammond's court was crowded for the preliminary hearing in early June, where Collins tried to prove an alibi and Mrs. Standley said she was certain of him. Bound over to the district court, he stayed in the county jail, unable to make bail.

His first trial opened before Judge Reed in late September, with many Black spectators in the courtroom who, the Eagle wrote, believed him innocent. The Eagle described the state's case as resting mostly on circumstantial evidence, while the defense argued that no crime had been committed and that Mrs. Standley could not have recognized Collins. That jury failed to agree.

A second trial began on November 12 after the court refused a continuance for an absent defense witness, Jerry Hart. Collins was found guilty, denied a new trial and sentenced on December 21 to nine years at hard labor in the penitentiary at Leavenworth.

The first reports came by wire from Kansas City and ran in Nebraska and Kansas papers from May 23 to early June under headlines such as "A Negro's Crime," "A Black Brute" and "Ravished by a Black Brute," before any suspect had been identified. No wire report of the threatened lynching itself appears in the coverage.

The Wichita Eagle reported the night at the jail under "Preparations for a Mob" in a plain tone, giving room to the Black men who came to guard the prisoner. Its court columns followed the case through two trials and gave the defense's arguments, though its sentencing notice stated as fact that Collins had raped Mrs. Standley. In October the Western Kansas World reprinted a Wichita Beacon item recalling the threats of lynching and the militia guard.

The Beacon, writing four months later, said that "several attempts" were made to get Collins out of jail and that the sheriff had to call out the state militia. The Eagle's report from the night itself describes only a rumored mob that never came, with the militia already in readiness, and is the closer account.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Collins
bases: A rumored mob planned to storm the Wichita jail and hang Collins, a jailed Black man accused of rape, and the sheriff, militia and armed citizens guarded the jail; no mob appeared and no one was hurt (A2, A11).

No one was killed: the Eagle reported that the expected mob never materialized and Collins was later tried and sentenced (A2, A14); the episode was a threatened lynching over a rape accusation (A1, A2, A11).

The wire report of lynching talk (A1), the local Eagle's account of the night guard at the jail (A2) and the Beacon's later summary (A11) independently report the lynching threat, though they differ on whether any attempt was actually made.

framing.detail: Kansas and Nebraska papers ran the May 22 wire under 'A Black Brute. Assault Upon a Wichita Widow by a Negro Fiend' and 'Ravished by a Black Brute,' treating the unidentified assailant's guilt and race as fact.
The Eagle's 'Preparations for a Mob' described the jail guard without endorsing the mob, credited the preparations with deterring it, and noted Black men's resolve to protect the prisoner.
The Eagle's court reports called the evidence mostly circumstantial and recorded defense arguments, but its sentencing item stated as fact that Collins 'raped Mrs. Standley.'
